Underline what the author wants you to believe. Then ask what would have to be true for the evidence to get you there.

    How to use it

    Work through the reasoning

    Put an abstract choice in plain words. Use the people and things in the argument.

    1. What's the conclusion? What does the author want me to believe?
    2. What did the evidence actually show? Keep that separate from what the author concludes.
    3. Which flaw is that? Then ask which choice says it in plain words. Review the wrong choices too.
    From our session

    You had it down to A and E. A says the counselor treats a way to get a motive as something you need to get one. E says the counselor took apart somebody else's argument and called their conclusion false. Where did the counselor do that? The counselor gave reasons for harsh criticism. There was no other argument to take apart.

    In the examples, green marks the evidence, gold marks the conclusion, and red marks the words that connect them.

    The five most common

    Start with these five

    Over half of flaw questions fall into these five fallacies. Learn what each one does, then look for it in the argument.

    Most common · 1 of 10

    Necessary vs. Sufficient

    What it is

    Presenting a conditional rule and then using it in an illegal backwards or opposite fashion to get to the conclusion (i.e. an illegal reversal or illegal negation). This is frequently the actual flaw on Flaw and Parallel Flaw questions.

    Examples
    People who have seen “The 13th” have a great understanding of the US prison system. Since Megan still hasn’t seen that documentary, she must have a poor understanding of the US prison system.
    People who have seen “The 13th” have a great understanding of the US prison system. Jane understands the US prison system really well, so clearly she has seen “The 13th.”
    Why it’s wrong

    A guaranteed way is not the only way. Megan could understand the prison system without seeing the film. Jane could understand it for the same reason. Neither conclusion follows from the rule.

    Spot it

    A rule gets reversed or negated, or enough becomes required.

    The right answer says
    • “takes a condition that is enough to bring about a result to be required for that result”
    • “treats an event that can cause a certain result as though that event is necessary to bring about that result”
    • “confuses a condition that is required for something with a condition that guarantees it”
    Don’t confuse it with · Causal

    “takes a correlation between two things as proof that one causes the other”

    Enough becomes required here. A causal flaw instead decides what caused something.

    From our session

    A guaranteed way is not the only way. You asked why it had to be harsh criticism. Gentle criticism could give someone a motive too. The word “cause” in a choice doesn't tell you which mistake the counselor made.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    A library course teaches everyone who takes it how to use the archive. Mina knows how to use the archive. She must have taken the course.
    What does the evidence show?

    A library course teaches everyone who takes it how to use the archive.

    Check your reasoning

    Mina could have learned from a librarian. The rule gives us one way to learn.

    Most common · 2 of 10

    Causal

    What it is

    Overconfidently concluding one possible causal interpretation of a curious fact, usually a correlation, when other possible interpretations exist.

    Example
    People who are enlisted in the military are more likely than those who haven't to have excellent physiques. Evidently, military recruitment officers select their future soldiers in large part based on the applicant’s fitness and strength.
    Why it’s wrong

    Soldiers tend to be fit. The author says recruiters chose them for their fitness. What else could explain the pattern? Training could have made them fit. People who play sports might also be more likely to enlist. Sometimes a pattern can be a coincidence.

    Spot it

    The evidence shows a pattern; the conclusion decides what caused it.

    The right answer says
    • “takes for granted that because two things occur together, one must have caused the other”
    • “fails to consider that the supposed effect may actually be the cause”
    • “overlooks the possibility that some other factor is responsible for both”
    Don’t confuse it with · Sampling

    “uses evidence drawn from a sample that is unlikely to be representative”

    Sampling questions who was counted. Causal questions why the pattern happened.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    Students who study in the library finish more assignments. Studying in the library must make students finish more assignments.
    What does the evidence show?

    Students who study in the library finish more assignments.

    Check your reasoning

    Students who plan their work might both choose the library and finish more. The pattern leaves that explanation open.

    Most common · 3 of 10

    Part vs. Whole

    What it is

    Assuming that a trait that is true of each part of a collective is therefore true of the whole, or vice versa.

    Examples
    The military is part of the government, and the military is conducted with lots of honor and discipline. Thus, the government overall is conducted with lots of honor and discipline.
    Since rat poison is very harmful if ingested, each ingredient in rat poison would be very harmful if ingested.
    Why it’s wrong

    The military's discipline doesn't tell us how the rest of the government operates. The poison example goes the other way. A harmful mixture could contain a harmless ingredient used as bait.

    Spot it

    A trait moves between the parts and the whole.

    The right answer says
    • “illicitly presumes that a whole must lack a certain quality if all of its parts lack that quality”
    • “presumes that a characteristic of a group as a whole is shared by each member of that group”
    • “reaches a conclusion about one member of a group merely on the basis of the performance of the group as a whole”
    Don’t confuse it with · Sampling

    “takes the condition of one member of a category to be representative of the category in general”

    Sampling uses some people to speak for others. Part versus whole concerns the parts and what they make up together.

    From our session

    You put it plainly: just because the team does well overall doesn't mean every player does well. That's the whole idea: the team's performance doesn't establish each player's performance.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    Each track on the album is short. So the album must be short.
    What does the evidence show?

    Each track on the album is short.

    Check your reasoning

    Twenty short tracks can add up to a long album.

    Most common · 4 of 10

    Unproven vs. Proven False

    What it is

    Acting like X must be false, either because there's no evidence that X is true, or because someone made a faulty argument for X being true.

    Examples
    Billy says that his uncle was related to Elvis, but he hasn't been able to connect them on Ancestry.com. Thus, Billy’s uncle was not related to Elvis.
    Some claim that the Atlanta Braves should change their name because they are the only major sports team that still has a Native American mascot. However, the Chicago Blackhawks still have a Native American mascot. Thus, the Braves should not change their name.
    Why it’s wrong

    A lack of evidence is not evidence of lacking. Failing to find the family connection doesn't prove there isn't one. The Braves argument points out a problem with one reason for changing the name. That doesn't settle whether the name should change.

    Spot it

    The author rejects a claim because proof is missing or an argument for it failed.

    The right answer says
    • “takes for granted that something that has not been proven to be true is for that reason shown to be false”
    • “takes lack of evidence for a claim as evidence undermining that claim”
    • “infers that a claim is false merely on the grounds that no satisfactory evidence for it has been offered”
    Don’t confuse it with · The mirror image

    “concludes that a claim is true merely on the grounds that it has not been proven false”

    Which claim does the author treat as settled? The same mistake can run in either direction.

    From our session

    You compared it to saying, “because I can't prove you're innocent, you're guilty.” You were right: failing to prove one side doesn't prove the other.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    We found no record that the tree was planted in 1902. It must have been planted in another year.
    What does the evidence show?

    We found no record that the tree was planted in 1902.

    Check your reasoning

    The record could be missing even if the tree was planted in 1902.

    Most common · 5 of 10

    Ad Hominem

    What it is

    Dismissing a point of view because the source has a biased interest or has conflicting past behavior.

    Examples
    My friend Sameer says that social workers would be better at responding to domestic abuse calls than would armed police officers. But we can ignore this notion, since Sameer is a social worker and so his industry would benefit were cities to make this switch.
    My running coach tells me I should stretch before every run, but she skipped stretching for twenty years. So I can ignore her advice about stretching.
    Why it’s wrong

    Sameer could benefit from the change and still be right. His interest doesn't tell us whether social workers would respond better. The coach could fail to follow her own advice and still give good advice.

    Spot it

    The author dismisses a claim by attacking its source.

    The right answer says
    • “attacks the people making an argument rather than addressing their argument”
    • “disputes a claim on the basis of a supposed motive for making the claim rather than by assessing the evidence relevant to the claim”
    • “rejects a claim merely on the grounds that its proponent holds another view inconsistent with it”
    Don’t confuse it with · Inappropriate Appeal

    “relies on the word of a scholar who is unqualified in the area in question”

    An appeal trusts a source without support. Ad Hominem dismisses a claim by attacking its source.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    A bus driver says the new route would cut travel time. Drivers want the route changed, so her claim is false.
    What does the evidence show?

    A bus driver says the new route would cut travel time.

    Check your reasoning

    The driver can want the change and be right about travel time.

    Not-so-common

    Know what the other five describe

    These show up less often as the flaw. Some, like the appeals, mostly show up as wrong answers.

    Not-so-common · 6 of 10

    Sampling

    What it is

    Extrapolating/generalizing too readily from a small sample, while failing to consider that the sample might be biased, too small, or unrepresentative.

    Examples
    Charlie, a staunch Republican, is from San Francisco and works for a theater company. Since Shelia is also from San Francisco and also works for a theater company, she is probably a staunch Republican too.
    Today’s youth prefer comic books to literature. After all, at a survey conducted at last year’s Comic-Con, over 85% of the young people surveyed reported liking comic books much more than novels.
    Why it’s wrong

    Sharing a city and a workplace doesn't establish a shared political view. And Comic-Con attracts people who like comics. Their preferences don't tell us what young people overall prefer.

    Spot it

    Evidence about a few people becomes a claim about others.

    The right answer says
    • “relies on the opinions of a group unlikely to be representative of the group at issue in the conclusion”
    • “bases an overly broad generalization on just a few instances”
    • “treats high school students from a particular medium-sized city as if they are representative of high school students nationwide”
    Don’t confuse it with · Part vs. Whole

    “assumes that what is true of each member of a group is true of the group as a whole”

    Ask whether the conclusion concerns other people or what the parts make up together.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    Everyone I asked at the chess club wants a chess tournament. So most students at school want one.
    What does the evidence show?

    Everyone I asked at the chess club wants a chess tournament.

    Check your reasoning

    Chess club members have more reason to want a chess tournament than students chosen across the school.

    Not-so-common · 7 of 10

    Inappropriate Appeal

    What it is

    Your evidence is a plea for sympathy, you cite an "authority" without establishing credibility, or you favor one source's opinion over another source's, without justifying your pick. Almost always wrong answers:

    Examples
    I know I was speeding, Officer, but you shouldn’t give me a ticket because it would ruin my Anniversary.
    The state geologist says the hillside behind the school is stable. But she’s wrong, for my neighbor says the ground there shifts.
    Why it’s wrong

    Ruining an anniversary gives the officer a reason to feel sympathy. It doesn't show the ticket is unwarranted. Why trust the neighbor over the geologist? The argument never establishes the neighbor's credibility or gives a reason to prefer that source.

    Spot it

    Sympathy or a source's opinion stands in for support, with no reason to trust that source.

    The right answer says
    • “treats a claim as true merely because many people believe it”
    • “accepts the view of someone who has no expertise on the matter at hand”
    • “appeals to emotion rather than offering evidence for its conclusion”
    Don’t confuse it with · Ad Hominem

    “attacks the person making the claim at issue rather than addressing the claim”

    An appeal trusts a source without support. Ad Hominem dismisses a claim by attacking its source.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    A famous actor says the old bridge can support trucks. The city can safely reopen it to trucks.
    What does the evidence show?

    A famous actor says the old bridge can support trucks.

    Check your reasoning

    The actor might know bridges. The argument gives us no reason to think so.

    Not-so-common · 8 of 10

    Circular Reasoning

    What it is

    The premise of an argument restates or assumes the conclusion.

    Example
    The LSAT is clearly the hardest grad school test, because all the other tests people take to go to grad school pale in comparison to the difficulty of the LSAT.
    Why it’s wrong

    Saying every other graduate test is easier already says the LSAT is the hardest. Would you already have to accept the conclusion to accept the premise? Here, yes. A weak or off-topic premise is a different problem.

    Spot it

    Accepting the premise already requires accepting the conclusion.

    The right answer says
    • “restates its conclusion and offers it as a reason”
    • “presupposes the truth of the conclusion it is attempting to establish”
    • “takes for granted the very conclusion it is trying to prove”
    Don’t confuse it with · An ordinary assumption

    “presupposes without justification that one event prevents another”

    It's circular only if accepting the premise already requires accepting the conclusion.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    This is the most reliable bus route. Every other route is less reliable than this one.
    What does the evidence show?

    This is the most reliable bus route.

    Check your reasoning

    To accept that every other route is less reliable, you already have to accept that this route is the most reliable.

    Not-so-common · 9 of 10

    Internal Contradiction

    What it is

    Something the author says undermines or contradicts something else they say.

    Example
    LSAT is an incredibly challenging test for anyone who takes it. However, if you commit to Eddie Spaghetti’s Steady LSAT Readiness protocol, you will soon be feeling like LSAT is no harder than a kindergarten spelling quiz.
    Why it’s wrong

    The word 'feeling' matters. A challenging test can feel easy to someone who's prepared, so the example can be read as consistent. A true contradiction requires two claims that cannot both hold. In the PCB question below, the author rejects any scientifically valid inference from a study, then uses that study as proof.

    Spot it

    The author relies on two claims that cannot both hold.

    The right answer says
    • “makes two claims that cannot both be true”
    • “its conclusion contradicts an implicit principle on which an earlier part of the argument is based”
    • “relies on premises that cannot all be true”
    Don’t confuse it with · Ad Hominem

    “rejects a claim merely on the grounds that its proponent holds another view inconsistent with it”

    Whose claims conflict? Here they're claims the author relies on together.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    A poll of three riders cannot tell us what most riders want. That same poll proves that most riders want later buses.
    What does the evidence show?

    A poll of three riders cannot tell us what most riders want.

    Check your reasoning

    The author rules out exactly the inference they then draw.

    Not-so-common · 10 of 10

    Equivocation

    What it is

    Using the same "term" or concept to mean two very different things.

    Example
    Some question whether Egypt condones Romania’s recent military buildup on their eastern border. But clearly Egypt sanctions this activity, since in the weeks following the Romanian military’s actions, Egypt issued sanctions against Romania.
    Why it’s wrong

    'Sanction' can mean approve, or it can refer to a penalty. Here the evidence says Egypt imposed penalties. Does that establish approval? No, the conclusion uses the other meaning.

    Spot it

    The same term changes meaning between the evidence and conclusion.

    The right answer says
    • “relies on a word that is used with two different meanings”
    • “uses a key term in two different senses”
    • “overlooks the possibility that the speaker is referring to two different kinds of right”
    Don’t confuse it with · A shift in terms

    “makes an irrelevant shift from discussing retail prices to discussing production costs”

    Find the term and state both meanings. Switching to a different term is a different problem.

    Practice

    Say what the evidence gives you. What would you still need to know?

    A feather is light. Light is what lets us see in a dark room. So a feather can help us see in the dark.
    What does the evidence show?

    A feather is light.

    Check your reasoning

    The first light means low in weight. The second means illumination.

    Your work

    What to do next

    1. Keep the list beside you during flaw practice. Name the mistake before reading the choices. You’ll get quicker as you see the same mistakes again.
    2. Review every choice. For each one you ruled out, say what it describes and point to where that would have happened in the argument.
